lineage: mutation of I0195 ('Contingency Recovery of Missed Rotable Repair Warranties'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Ramco Aviation (MRO/ERP software, warranty management module). White space: Caveat: this verdict rests on thin evidence. The WebSearch budget was exhausted (200 of 200) after the first two lookups. Every further search was refused, and I did not work around that limit. I could only fetch vendor homepages directly. I found no dedicated contingency-fee warranty auditor for rotable repair claims. I also could not rule one out, because I could not run Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or 'startup + key terms' searches. Vendor pages I checked (Trax eMRO, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000, CAMP) showed no warranty-claims features on their homepages, but homepage silence is weak evidence. I could not check IFS Maintenix (HTTP 429). Gaps that look unserved: (1) an outsourced, success-fee service that reads unstructured repair-invoice PDFs and joins them to removal records. This is the cross-system join the idea describes. (2) Small and mid-size operators such as regionals, Part 135 fleets and air-ambulance operators, which sit below the large ERP buyers Ramco targets. (3) The adjacent leaks, meaning no-fault-found fees within warranty, unreturned core penalties and turnaround-time guarantee credits. None of the vendor pages I read mention these. Unverified risks from my own domain knowledge, not from research: power-by-the-hour and maintenance-service-plan contracts remove warranty exposure for many small fleets. Shop warranty terms are often short and carry exclusions. Getting AP and maintenance-system exports from a small operator is hard. The addressable market may be small. Someone should check all of these before building. | How this version avoids them: Ramco is a one-sided ERP module for large operators. This is a neutral layer between companies, which one company's ERP cannot be. The Trax, Veryon/Rusada, Pentagon 2000 and CAMP homepages showed no claims network. OEM warranty portals, as far as I know, run one way, from the OEM to its customers, and cover the OEM's own new-part warranty, not third-party repair warranties. That is a domain-knowledge assumption to check, as is whether ATA Spec 2000-type standards already cover warranty claims. The first product also needs no maintenance-system integration, and starts with a segment (pools) that has no PBH shield.

title: Rural Sales Commons: Pay Retiring Appraisers for Comps
one_liner: Invert the idea: instead of retirees paying to leave, pay them for their verified sales books and build the private sales-price registry that non-disclosure states lack, sold first to practicing rural appraisers and later to AVM, lender and assessor buyers.
customer: Supply (paid): retiring and retired certified residential appraisers in roughly a dozen non-disclosure states (for example TX, UT, ID, MT, WY, NM, KS, LA, MS, ND), starting with Texas. Demand: practicing rural appraisers first (subscription), then AVM and hybrid-valuation vendors, rural lenders' collateral-risk teams, county assessors for ratio studies, and eventually programs expanding alternative valuations.
problem: In non-disclosure states, sale prices are not in public deed records. For non-MLS rural sales (FSBO, family transfers, auctions, seller-financed land-with-house), the only record of price is often an appraiser's own phone-confirmation notes and comp files. When the appraiser retires, that sales book is thrown out or dies on a hard drive. Practicing appraisers then struggle to find defensible comps, AVMs and desktop valuations are weakest exactly there (hypothesis to test), and human appraisers stay indispensable and scarce.
solution: Wedge product: a 'Rural Comp Finder' subscription for practicing appraisers in one region, built from a paid capture program. (1) Sales Book Capture: a 2-day white-glove engagement in which we ingest the retiree's comp libraries (a la mode or ClickFORMS exports, spreadsheets, paper binders) with LLM parsing. We keep only transaction facts (date, price, terms, property characteristics, verification source and method), plus the retiree's own adjustment grids and market-area notes. Client and borrower identities never enter the system, and MLS-derived fields are tagged and excluded. The retiree signs a license and certifies what is theirs. (2) Product: county-level search showing each verified sale with provenance (who confirmed, how, when) and a confidence grade, plus a paired-sales adjustment library. (3) Contributor loop: active appraisers who add confirmed sales get a discount, so the commons refreshes after the retirees are gone. (4) Later products: API and data licenses to AVM and hybrid vendors, lenders and county assessors, positioned as ground truth for validating AVMs and alternative valuations.
why_now: About 6-7k appraisers a year are expected to leave (31% of a roughly 65k workforce within 3 years per WorkingRE), and each exit destroys a sales book permanently. UAD 3.6 (mandatory Nov 2, 2026) pushes the industry toward structured data. EO 14393 expands alternative valuations, which need ground truth in thin markets. LLM extraction of messy comp files (old exports, PDFs, handwritten binders) became cheap enough in 2025-26 to make capture affordable.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $39-59 per month per region for active appraisers (contributors pay less). Data licenses of about $25-120k per state per year to AVM and hybrid vendors and lenders, and $15-40k per year to assessors (all unvalidated). Retirees are paid $1,500-3,000 upfront plus a 20-25% royalty pool shared by verified contribution, and that payout is our main cost of goods. Rough plan (assumptions): 20 retirees x about $2,000 is $40k to acquire perhaps 50-100k verified records. 300 subscribers by month 12 is roughly $210k ARR before any data licenses.
non_obvious_insight: The parent asks retirees to pay, but a retiree is a supplier with a ticking clock. Each exit permanently deletes an asset that no later entrant can recreate, and scraping cannot reach it because the value is provenance: who confirmed this price, how and when. First to sign the last generation of phone-confirming appraisers cornered a resource competitors cannot buy once it is gone. Practicing appraisers contributing new confirmed sales gives the commons a network effect that outlasts the retirees. The moat is the counsel-designed data model (provenance tagging, MLS exclusion, client stripping), which turns legal risk into a barrier to fast followers. Because retirees are paid, the parent's unproven willingness-to-pay problem disappears and no earn-out or client transfer is needed.
first_30_days: Gating step: a counsel memo on MLS license terms, the USPAP Confidentiality Rule, GLBA and state board views, and stop or redesign if the extractable data set is too thin. Interview 15 retirees and 15 active appraisers in Texas and ask to see their comp books. Buy 5 sales books at $1,500 as paid pilots, parse them with an LLM pipeline, and tag provenance and MLS-derived rows. Run a blind coverage test on one rural county: how many verified non-MLS sales in the last 5 years the commons holds versus what an active appraiser or an AVM can find. Show the test to 3 AVM or hybrid-valuation vendors and 3 rural lenders and ask for letters of intent. Pre-sell a $39 per month beta to 30 active appraisers. Because the web-search budget ran out, also verify in week 1 whether Cotality, ATTOM or any appraiser comp-sharing group already sells verified non-MLS sales in non-disclosure states.
lineage: mutation of I1039 ('Retirement-in-a-Box for Exiting Appraisers'), type: 10x-or-inverted
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: LIA Administrators (Appraisal Institute-endorsed E&O program), OREP (Appraisal Insurance), a la mode TOTAL / Cotality (also ACI, ClickFORMS), Aloft Appraisal. White space: No company found that bundles the four pieces (workfile custody plus subpoena and board-inquiry response, tail, local-knowledge capture, direct-lender client handoff to a supervised successor). Searches for retiring-appraiser succession services, workfile custodian services, and appraiser practice brokers returned only DIY articles from WorkingRE, McKissock, Appraisal Today and NAR.

Specific white space that survives:
(1) Third-party workfile custody and retrieval (agent-of-record for subpoenas and board requests) for retired or deceased appraisers. USPAP requires retention and retrievability for 5+ years, with regulators able to act later, and no dedicated vendor was found. Software vendors and cloud storage only store files, and nobody answers a subpoena for you.
(2) Local, rural or community-lender-funded succession. Aloft, Valligent and Solidifi are national or AMC-centric, not local continuity for a single county.
(3) The retiree-as-mentor stipend and earn-out structure, which none of the trainee programs use.

Specific weaknesses in the idea:
(a) The 'tail is frightening and costly' pain is largely solved for long-tenured appraisers by free LIA and OREP retirement tails. The paid pain is limited to those with short E&O tenure, gaps, or sub-5-year policies. Tail brokerage commissions are therefore thin.
(b) Fee-splitting and finder's-fee rules. Minnesota (82B.20) bans commission-splitting, rebates and finder's fees with appraisers, and other states have similar rules. An earn-out on inherited client revenue and a 20-30% take on trainee fees may be illegal in some states unless structured as a sale of a business or as employment.
(c) Supervisor-of-record is not passive. State rules limit trainee counts (Aloft cites 3 per supervisor), require certification in good standing and the supervisor's own E&O, and make the supervisor take full responsibility. A retiree who stays on as supervisor is not really retired and keeps license, CE and E&O costs.
(d) Client transferability is weak. Appraisal Today notes practices under $200K are 'buying a job', and residential lender relationships are 'fickle'. Most practices sell at 0.33-0.5x revenue with seller financing, and AMC-dependent revenue is not transferable.
(e) Pipeline substitutes are growing: PAREA, AXIS/CRN trainee-inspection reform, Valligent and Aloft paying supervisors. | How this version avoids them: None of the parent's competitors sell data: LIA and OREP sell tail coverage, a la mode stores each user's own files, and Aloft, Valligent, Solidifi, AXIS and PAREA are trainee and supervisor programs, so this idea leaves the trainee, supervisor and client-handoff lane entirely. Aloft, Reggora and AMC-side firms are more likely buyers of the data than competitors. Incumbent data vendors (Cotality, ATTOM, MLS aggregators) depend on MLS feeds and recorder data and would have to buy retiree confirmations one appraiser at a time, which does not fit their scale (unverified, to check in week 1). The design avoids fee-splitting law because no appraisal fee or client revenue is shared, avoids supervisor-licensing issues, and avoids weak client transferability because no clients move.

title: Rotor Rescue as Scrapyard Deal-Sourcing Engine
one_liner: Use the pay-per-rotor magnet program as the free-to-yard front door that surfaces retiring scrapyard owners and gives search-fund buyers a day-one margin lever and guaranteed magnet supply.
customer: Laid-off mid-career managers with $100-300K who pay cohort tuition to buy and run a yard. Scrapyard, motor-shop and appliance-recycler owners, both as rotor sellers and as retiring owners. Rare-earth magnet recyclers that need domestic feed. SBA lenders as a channel.
problem: The accelerator's scarce input is proprietary, fairly priced deal flow (brokered scrap-yard listings are thin) and a differentiated value-creation story for lenders and sellers. Rotor Rescue's scarce inputs are trust with thousands of skeptical independent yards and aggregate volume, and recyclers such as Cyclic already court suppliers directly.
solution: Phase 1: run Rotor Rescue in 2-3 states with a loaner gauss meter and a price sheet by motor model, paying yards per unit and aggregating lots for recyclers. Each enrolled yard reveals throughput, mix and owner age, so the program flags retirement-age owners. Phase 2: cohort members get first look at flagged yards, a permit-transfer and environmental diligence pack, SBA-lender introductions, and a ready 'magnet program' they can run on day one in the acquired yard. First sellable product: cohort seats at $4-6K that include the Rotor Rescue playbook and pre-sourced sell-side LOIs.
why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is failing (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies), while permitted, cash-flowing yards look safe. DOE announced $134M for critical-mineral demonstrations in June 2026, and DoD-backed magnet plants create domestic pull and funded recyclers that need feed.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition of $4-6K per seat. Buy-side success fee of $25-50K or 1.5-2% at close. 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Spread on assayed magnet feed sold to recyclers, plus a small SaaS fee for the identification and price app. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: A yard that you pay every month for rotors trusts you, and your purchase log is a quality-of-earnings proxy for its volume and mix. Retiring owners rarely list with brokers; they tell whoever already writes them checks. That makes Rotor Rescue a proprietary deal-sourcing channel disguised as a price-discovery service. In the other direction, an owned portfolio of yards turns the magnet-feed aggregation problem into contracted supply, which a national recycler would rather buy from than chase yard by yard.
first_30_days: Pull permit and owner-age lists for two states and buy 5 gauss meters. Visit 10 yards, measure 200 units and build the price sheet. Get an offtake LOI from one magnet recycler and pay 3 yards on the first 50 units. Run a webinar for laid-off managers ('buy a yard that already has a magnet program') to enroll about 10 for the first cohort. Ask the yards you visit which owners want an exit, sign two sell-side LOIs, and line up an environmental consultant and one SBA lender.
lineage: hybrid of I0626 + I0939 (Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards + Rotor Rescue: Scrapyard Magnet Pick-and-Pay). Why stronger: The accelerator gets proprietary deal flow and a concrete margin-improvement thesis at day one, which is the hardest thing for a first-time searcher to show a lender or seller. Rotor Rescue gets trusted access to yards, guaranteed volume through acquired yards, and a second revenue line that does not depend on rare-earth prices. Each side removes the other's biggest customer-acquisition cost.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Search Fund Accelerator (SFA), Kingsway Search Xcelerator (KSX), Codie Sanchez / Contrarian Thinking ('boring business' acquisition education), University ETA programs and search fund ecosystem (Stanford GSB, Kellogg, WashU Olin, Yale, Cleveland ETA program). White space: I found no scrap, recycling or transfer-station-specific acquisition accelerator. Every searcher or ETA program I could verify is sector-agnostic, and none packages this asset class for a first-time buyer. That is limited evidence. The session's 200-call WebSearch budget was already spent. I fell back on Google News RSS, the Hacker News API, the Federal Register API and direct fetches, and could not reach Crunchbase, Product Hunt, Reddit, Searchfunder or BizBuySell.

What looks unserved:
1. A vertical diligence and financing pack for sub-$5M scrap and recycling yards. It would cover Phase I/II and fire-history checks, insurance, permit transferability and offtake contracts. Horizontal ETA programs leave that to each buyer. Fire and insurance risk is live: EMR's Camden yard was shut after 15 fires in six years (NJ PEN, 29 May 2026), Resource Recycling wrote 'Battery fire risk isn't going away. Insurance is responding' (24 Feb 2026), and a 9,000-car Idaho salvage yard burned (Yahoo, 19 Jun 2026).
2. A succession desk for owner-run yards. Nothing I found targets ReMA-type family operators with a packaged successor, and the big consolidators only want larger yards.
3. A permit-and-owner-age target list. Nothing I found offers one for scrap dealers.

The premise needs two corrections:
- The BIS rule is real. It is a temporary final rule, published 6 Aug 2026 and effective 27 Aug 2026. However, it covers only black mass and tungsten waste and scrap, not ordinary ferrous or nonferrous yards (Federal Register 2026-16078). The 'domestic scrap re-rating' story is much narrower than the pitch implies.
- The idea leans on 'laid-off managers with $100-300K'. That is a crowded buyer-education market, with Codie Sanchez, Kingsway and the universities all courting the same buyers. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Cyclic Materials, HyProMag USA (CoTec / Mkango JV), ERI (Electronics Recyclers International), Noveon Magnetics. White space: Evidence caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 of 200) was exhausted, so I ran zero successful web searches and relied on direct page fetches of about 20 company and source URLs. Several were 404, 503 or blocked. Coverage of forums, RFPs, Crunchbase, Product Hunt and open-source tools is therefore missing. Treat this as a partial check, not a clean bill of health.\n\nWhat remains unserved, judged from the company pages I could read:\n(1) A yard-facing price and identification product. No fetched page (Cyclic, HyProMag, ReElement, Ionic, Noveon) publishes a payout by motor make and model, a magnet-mass lookup, or a handheld gauss-meter workflow for yard staff. Cyclic's supplier page explicitly gives no pricing, logistics or ID tools ('contact us to get started').\n(2) The long tail of small and mid-size auto shredders, motor rebuilders, elevator and industrial motor shops, and e-bike hub-motor scrap. ERI is anchored on e-waste and the OEM/ITAD channel, and Cyclic's named categories are drive motors, HDDs, robotics, defense and wind. Elevator, servo and e-bike hub motors are not named.\n(3) Chain-of-custody and assay data for defense-traceable lots.\n\nWhere the idea is weak: the buyers are building their own procurement. Cyclic takes whole units without dismantling, so the 'mobile pull cell' adds little. Cyclic and HyProMag have stated supply pipelines and can capture the aggregator margin by paying yards directly once yards know what they hold. The spread-based aggregator model is exposed to that squeeze. The durable wedge is the data and identification layer.

title: Neutral Ground Baseline for Foundation Projects
one_liner: A developer-paid, two-sided satellite baseline of every neighboring tower, delivered at the same time to neighbors and insurers, and sold as a line item by the geotech and vibration-monitoring firms already on the job.
customer: Payer: mid-size South Florida condo developers and general contractors (and their deep-foundation subcontractors) on projects with pile-driving, dewatering or deep excavation within about 300 m of occupied towers. Co-buyers: builders-risk and CGL underwriters, MGAs and wholesale brokers who insure those projects. Channel: geotech and vibration-monitoring engineering firms who already write the monitoring plan and can resell.
problem: Neighbor claims are the tail risk of urban high-rise foundation work. Vibration and settlement claims, injunction threats and stop-work fights can add months of construction-loan carry on a $150M-$400M tower. The developer's own crack survey is discounted as self-serving. Underwriters have no independent evidence of pre-existing condition, so they price the whole neighborhood as worst case, or add sublimits, higher deductibles or exclusions for adjacent-property damage. The UM study showed many towers were already sinking at mm/yr for reasons unrelated to any neighbor. Developers cannot prove that, and neither can anyone else.
solution: Neighbor Ledger. At permit or early foundation stage, process the archive for every building in the influence zone (typically 15-40 towers) and issue a neutral baseline package. It goes the same day to (a) the developer and its insurer and (b) each neighboring association through a read-only portal. Neighbors get a free 3-page report on their own tower, which gives them evidence and a reason to stop fighting the permit. Timestamps and data hashes are anchored, so neither side can dispute the record. During construction, a monthly delta report flags any tower whose motion departs from its own trend or from control towers. When a claim is filed, a dispute packet is generated within days. A rule is written into every contract: the company gives identical data to both sides and never testifies for either. Expert work goes to an independent geodesist panel. Priced fixed per project and sold as an add-on line item on the geotech firm's monitoring contract.
why_now: Miami's high-rise foundation boom is running against an unusually alert neighbor base: the 2024 UM study was widely covered, Marenas spent about $20K on sensors after a neighbor started work, and the Estructura June 2026 campaign has associations asking developers for data. Post-Surfside underwriters demand structural documentation, and softening reinsurance capacity makes MGAs hungry for differentiated loss-control tools. Processing cost has collapsed with free OPERA DISP-S1, Sentinel-1 and NISAR data.
revenue_model: $18K baseline per project at permit, plus $2.5K/month during foundation and superstructure phases (about 18 months), so about $60-65K per project against a $150M+ build. Reseller share of 20-25% to the geotech or vibration firm. Insurers and MGAs get a portfolio loss-control dashboard as a $25-50K/year program license, in exchange for a premium credit or a warranty requiring the ledger. Assumed 30-40 new high-rise foundation starts per year across Miami-Dade, Broward and Palm Beach (verify from permit data), so about 12 projects in year one at roughly $700K. Expansion to Tampa, Orlando and Houston follows once insurers accept it.
non_obvious_insight: The parent's flaw was that boards may not want to know. Here the party with the strongest need to know is the developer, whose worst nightmare is a false or mistaken damage claim. A baseline showing the neighbor was already sinking is worth more to the developer than to the neighbor. Neutrality is the product: one record both sides accepted is worth more than two competing reports, the way an escrow agent is worth more than two lawyers. Because every competitor is on one side, refusing to take a side is a position none of them can copy without losing their existing clients. Once about 10 projects and two insurers rely on ledgers, a city or county can make a settlement baseline a permit condition, as some European cities require for deep excavation next to older buildings. That would turn a product into infrastructure (hedge: verify local precedent).
first_30_days: Week 1: list the 6-8 geotech and vibration-monitoring firms with active Miami-Dade or Broward jobs, using their public monitoring plans and permit files. Build unsolicited Neighbor Ledgers for 5 currently active sites from free data. Week 2: pitch each firm 'add this as a line item, you keep 25%, we do all the work.' Meet 4 builders-risk and CGL wholesale brokers and MGAs with a one-page loss-control pitch and one question: would you give a premium credit or require it? Weeks 3-4: close one developer pilot at half price ($9K) on a site in early foundation stage, in exchange for an underwriter introduction, and sign one geotech reseller. Kill test: if no geotech firm will bundle it and no underwriter will credit it, drop the model.

This is fixed-price, bilateral and neutral, and priced for mid-size developers. Their client model conflicts with sharing data with neighbors, and ours depends on it. title: Family Bank: Bank of Mom and Dad, Papered
one_liner: A family office's real job is governance and records, not investing; for $20/mo, give ordinary parents and adult children a promissory-note, autopay and sibling-fairness ledger for the money that already flows between them.
customer: Parents aged 55-75 who lend or give money to adult children (down-payment help, car, tuition, debt payoff, business start), sold as a pair with the adult child (28-45). Elder-law attorneys, mortgage brokers and credit unions are referral channels.
problem: Family lending is handshake-based. Zero-interest loans over $10k invite imputed-interest questions. Gifts above the $19,000 annual exclusion (2026) need Form 709 filings. Medicaid's 60-month look-back treats gifts and forgiven loans as transfers. Mortgage lenders want documented gift letters. Siblings fight at inheritance over who got what because nobody kept records. NAR's 2025 profile shows the median first-time buyer is 40 and 22% received a gift or loan from relatives or friends.
solution: A guided flow decides gift vs loan and generates a note at or above the AFR (August 2026: 4.10% short, 4.35% mid, 4.92% long). ACH autopay collects and pays, and both sides get annual interest statements. A December 'forgiveness engine' forgives up to the exclusion with proper letters. A sibling ledger records every advancement so estates can equalize. Flags fire for Form 709 and Medicaid look-back exposure, and there is a mortgage-ready gift-letter generator plus one-click export to the family's estate attorney. Attorney review is an add-on.
why_now: Median first-time buyer age hit 40 (a record), housing costs push more family help, and long-term-care costs make the Medicaid look-back a live worry for boomer parents. Instant-payment and bank-linking rails make autopay cheap. The 2026 federal estate exemption is $15M, so for most families the value is peace and records, not tax planning.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family (up to 3 active loans); $49 document packs for the free-to-paid funnel; $149 attorney review add-on with referral fees; optional servicing fee; later, a pooled family reserve product.
non_obvious_insight: The killer feature is not the loan, it is the sibling ledger. Most family money fights are about unequal treatment nobody can prove, and family offices solve this with an advancement ledger that ordinary families never get. The loan-vs-gift label is also the pivot point for tax and Medicaid consequences, so classification is the paid moment.
first_30_days: Ship a free AFR calculator and note generator aimed at 'family loan agreement' searches, and sell $49 document packs. Convert 5% to the $20/mo servicing tier. Line up 3 elder-law attorneys who receive leads and review notes. Target 50 paying families.

title: Keep-the-Amps: Electrical Carve-Out for Plant Liquidations
one_liner: A 3,000-dollar electrician-verified 'in-place value memo' sold to industrial liquidators, trustees' counsel and corporate closure teams, so the switchgear and transformers are carved out of the equipment auction and sold with the real estate as a powered shell.
customer: Wedge: the 15-30 mid-size Midwest industrial liquidation auctioneers, and the panel trustees, receivers' counsel and corporate-real-estate disposition managers who hire them when a plant with at least 2 MW of service goes dark in OH, PA, MI or IN. Not manufacturers, not brokers.
problem: A plant liquidation has two teams that never talk. The equipment auctioneer sells presses, CNCs and often the switchgear, bus duct and transformers as used-equipment or scrap lots. The real-estate side lists square feet and dock doors. The energized service is the scarce asset (large transformers run about 128 weeks, switchgear 44-90+ weeks, so a buyer who has to replace them loses a year or more), and it is destroyed or stripped in the gap between the two teams. The trustee or seller has a fiduciary or financial duty to maximise proceeds but no document showing what the gear is worth in place versus removed. A secured mortgage lender and an equipment lender may also be fighting over what is a fixture.
solution: Sell one fixed-scope deliverable, the 'Powered-Shell Memo', in 8 days: (1) licensed electrician's one-day walk-through with one-line diagram, nameplates, gear age, thermography and spare capacity; (2) a carve-out schedule marking every item of electrical infrastructure as 'stays with the building' or 'safe to sell', with in-place value (replacement cost plus lead-time cost) against scrap and used-lot value; (3) utility service status (energized, disconnected, minimum-bill exposure) and a one-line check of air and wastewater permit status (shutdown, fees current, notification-only transfer), demoted to a checkbox because Ohio EPA transfer is easy; (4) a buyer-agnostic data-room cut that a data-center, battery, cold-storage or manufacturing buyer can underwrite. The fee is a flat cost line in the auction budget, paid from proceeds at closing, so the estate needs no upfront cash.
why_now: Buyers are paying for existing energized shells (TeraWulf/Anthropic's $19B lease on a shuttered aluminum plant, the former Goodyear plant in Akron running about 150 MW), and transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in years. Plant closures and manufacturer distress continue in 2026, so supply of dead plants is steady. Before the AI-power scramble a stripped switchgear lineup was worth scrap; now it is worth a year of a buyer's schedule.
revenue_model: $3,000 flat per plant (electrician cost about $1,300, analyst about 4 hours, roughly 55% gross margin), paid at closing or as a budgeted line in the liquidation. Add-ons: $1,200 buyer-ready data-room cut, $9,000 for multi-plant corporate closures (3-5 sites), and a $6k-$12k annual retainer for auctioneers who want a standing right to use the memo in their pitches. No percentage of sale price and no brokerage, which avoids the licence problem and the conflict the parent's success fee had. Later: license the anonymised gear-and-value dataset. Bottom-up: 150 to 250 qualifying Midwest industrial disposals a year at $3k-$4k is about $0.5M-$1M of report revenue for one small team before retainers, which is enough to fund the next two offspring-style expansions, not a venture-scale market by itself.
non_obvious_insight: The thing that destroys the power asset in a dead plant is the equipment auction itself, not neglect. The liquidator is paid to turn gear into cash quickly, the real-estate broker never sees the gear list, and nobody owns the question 'is the switchgear worth more bolted to the building?'. The memo is not a report on the building, it is a decision document that changes what goes in the auction catalogue, and it gives the trustee defensible cover for keeping it out.
first_30_days: Week 1: pull 24 months of WARN closure notices for OH/PA/MI/IN, PACER Chapter 7/11 filings by manufacturers with real property, and county receivership dockets, and cross-check against Ohio EPA facility status to list about 60 dark plants with 2 MW or more. Week 2: call 15 regional liquidation auctioneers and 10 trustee counsel with one offer, a free first memo on their next live liquidation in exchange for a written case study and permission to anonymise the data. Weeks 3-4: hire one electrician for two walk-throughs at about $150 per hour; deliver memos; ask one secured mortgage lender to accept a memo as a fixture-line exhibit. Success test: at least one auctioneer pulls electrical gear from a catalogue, and two of the next three mandates pay $3,000 at closing.

White space: Nobody I found productises a building-level, physically verified 'inside-the-fence' record for dead Midwest plants. That record would cover the electrician-verified main service size, voltage, gear age and nameplates, spare capacity, slab and crane-rail condition, the state of the existing air and wastewater permits, and a utility will-serve letter, all in a scored, comparable format sold before the deal. The funded players (LandGate, Enverus, GridCARE, Paces) work at the substation and grid level and are aimed at data centers. Utility and state databases (JobsOhio, AEP, FirstEnergy, ZoomProspector) verify sites and utility service, not building gear or permit status. Scout and Brownfield.ai are the closest competitors, but they look desktop- and network-led with no per-building inspection, and I found no evidence they carry electrician-verified data. The idea's weaker points: the Ohio permit-transferability wedge is thin (see evidence), and it is unproven that brokers will pay $1.5k-$3.5k. | How this version avoids them: It is not a listing or parcel-scoring database, so it steps around Brownfield.ai, Scout, ZoomProspector, LandGate and Enverus, which all sell search or grid-level screening to buyers. The payer is the seller side at the moment of disposition, which none of them serve, and JobsOhio, AEP and FirstEnergy databases are free but verify sites and service, not gear or carve-out decisions. PCA and electrical inspection firms give buyers a compliance-style ampacity line; nobody gives a seller a valued in-place versus scrap schedule tied to the auction terms. The permit-transferability wedge that was thin in the parent is reduced to a checkbox, and the success fee is dropped.

title: Human Bench Network for AI Agents
one_liner: An API-fronted network of laid-off expert bench scientists who run ad hoc wet-lab experiments for AI agents and return machine-readable execution records.
customer: AI-first biotechs, AI-for-science startups and university groups (5-60 people, seed to Series B) that run agent swarms but have no wet lab; later, programs adjacent to frontier labs.
problem: Agent swarms now propose far more experiments than anyone can run. Anthropic's run went from 200,000+ reverse transcriptases to 20 candidates using ~950 agents in 21 hours. Stanford's Virtual Biotech (37,000 agents, Science, Sept 17, 2026) says the next step is testing findings in real labs. Cloud labs and robots handle fixed assays, but not ad hoc molecular biology: Anthropic itself found robotics less conducive to ad hoc workflows and kept human scientists at the bench. Human review and bench work are the bottleneck.
solution: Ticketed experiments through an API or MCP endpoint. The agent proposes a protocol and a senior scientist does feasibility triage. A vetted contractor then runs it at sublet or surplus benches, BSL-1/2 only. Each job returns a signed record that separates AI proposal, human edit and physical execution (deviations, photos, instrument logs, raw data). Fixed price per experiment. Start with commodity molecular biology: cloning, small-scale expression and purification, ELISA/BLI/qPCR, enzyme activity, bacterial and cell-culture assays.
why_now: Frontier labs and Stanford now say publicly that bench execution is the bottleneck. BioSpace tracks 15,000+ biopharma job cuts across 50+ companies in 2026, which supplies skilled hands. The OpenAI Foundation plans to distribute $1B by year-end through Public Data for Health, which creates grant-funded demand for data generation. Lab Manager notes there is no sign-off standard for AI-directed experiments, and this record format supplies one. Anthropic has said it wants to work with other scientists.
revenue_model: $1.5-8k per experiment at roughly 35-45% gross margin, monthly retainers with minimum volumes for agent-heavy customers, and a premium for 48-hour turnaround. The platform keeps a take rate on contractor labor.
non_obvious_insight: Compute is now nearly free compared with bench throughput, and robots failed as the universal answer because real biology is ad hoc. The defensible assets are a pre-vetted pool of humans and a structured execution record that agents can learn from. Humans become the last-mile actuator for AI. Adaptyv and cloud labs cover single fixed assays; nobody sells the long tail of one-off experiments.
first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 laid-off molecular biologists in Boston, SF and San Diego through layoff trackers and alumni groups. Rent 2-3 sublet benches or surplus CRO benches. Define three ticket types with fixed prices. Pitch 10 AI protein-design and agent startups and close 3-5 pilots. Aim for the first 20 paid experiments and publish the sample record schema.

title: Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue
one_liner: Find the 'ghost parcels' and slow big meters that leak revenue out of a utility, using assessor rolls, building footprints, imagery and billing data, and get paid 20-30% of what is recovered so the city risks nothing.
customer: City, county and district water and sewer utilities with 10k-200k connections. The buyer is the finance director or utility director who is facing a council fight over the next rate increase.
problem: Utilities are raising rates 5-10% a year to fund PFAS treatment, lead line replacement and aging pipes, and councils are pushing back on affordability. Meanwhile revenue leaks out in places nobody owns: structures with no water account (unpermitted ADUs on shared meters, converted garages, fire and irrigation taps never billed), commercial compound meters that are 20-30 years old and under-register at low flows, meters swapped without the account being updated, stopped or zero-read accounts that never get investigated, and sewer-only accounts billed off a bad water read. The customer information system, the GIS parcel layer and the assessor roll sit in different departments. Nobody owns the join, and nobody has staff to do it.
solution: Join the utility's account list and consumption history to the assessor roll (building sq ft, units, use code), permits, open building-footprint datasets and aerial imagery (pools, irrigated area, added structures). Build an expected-consumption model by parcel. Rank the mismatches: no account at all, consumption far below expected, sudden step-downs after a meter change, and large meters whose low-flow profile looks wrong. A small field crew and a meter-test partner verify the top leads. The utility gets a documented recovery list with legal-ready evidence, back-billing calculations that respect the state's limits, and a meter-replacement plan. The firm takes 20-30% of first-year recovered incremental revenue.
why_now: Rate shock and affordability politics in 2025-26 make 'recover what we're owed before raising rates' an easy story for council. Open building-footprint datasets and cheap vision AI make expected-consumption modeling accessible to a two-person team, and utilities that finished smart-meter rollouts now have interval data that has never been analyzed for revenue. Contingency work also clears procurement easily because there is no upfront cost.
revenue_model: Contingency of 20-30% on the first 12-24 months of recovered annualized revenue, plus a fixed fee for a meter-testing and replacement plan. Later, a recurring SaaS monitor ($1-3 per 100 accounts per month). Optional referral fees from meter and test vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The leak that matters is not in the pipe. Large commercial meters are about 10-20% of accounts but 40-60% of revenue, and the oldest ones quietly under-register the low flows that hospitals, hotels and factories use all night. The utility never sees this loss because the meter is the thing measuring it.
first_30_days: Pick a county whose assessor roll and building footprints are downloadable and whose utility publishes or will release account addresses (public-records request). Run a free scan and generate 20 named addresses with expected versus billed usage. Cold-email finance directors at five utilities with 'we'll show you 20 unbilled addresses before you sign anything'. Sign the first contingency contract with a city that has a rate hearing scheduled, and verify leads with a hired meter-testing subcontractor.

title: Retailer-Mandated Vulnerability Desk, Paid by Suppliers
one_liner: EU retailers and distributors put the desk on their approved-provider list for connected private-label and marketplace products, and their non-EU suppliers pay per SKU family, the way suppliers already pay retailer-nominated test labs, while the retailer gets a live exposure dashboard for its whole connected catalogue.
customer: Mandating party: product-compliance heads at mid-size EU consumer-electronics, DIY, sports (e-bikes), toy and discount retailers and distributors with 50-2,000 connected SKUs, including own-brand ranges. Payers: the 20-200 non-EU suppliers and ODMs behind those SKUs, each paying for the product families it sells to that retailer.
problem: A retailer that sells connected products under its own name is treated as the CRA manufacturer (to confirm with counsel), and an importer or distributor must chase unreachable non-EU suppliers when a vulnerability appears. Retailers have no view of which of their 1,800 connected SKUs contain the component in this morning's exploited-vulnerability headline. Their suppliers will not share firmware willingly and cannot show a 24h capability. The parent's problem is that small makers will not buy a desk they see as insurance. Here the party with the pain is not the party with the budget, and the retailer holds the leverage over the supplier.
solution: Product 1 is a retailer-paid 'Connected Range Exposure Baseline'. The desk collects firmware for 25-50 SKUs, which the retailer can compel from suppliers. It unpacks them, builds the component lists, checks current exposure to KEV/EUVD, tests each supplier's vulnerability-contact deliverability, and delivers a supplier-requirement clause for the next supplier manual. Product 2 is the ongoing service. The retailer's supplier manual names the desk (and any equivalent that passes its audit) as an approved provider. Each supplier enrols product families and the desk becomes its AR and 24/7 filing service, with stack-pooled triage. The retailer sees a live dashboard: for each SKU, affected, not affected or unknown, with supplier response time, supporting delist or recall decisions and its own regulatory file. The desk's fan-out model is reused, but the sales motion is one retailer mandate that brings in many suppliers.
why_now: CRA reporting has been live since 11 Sep 2026 and retailer supplier manuals are being rewritten ahead of Dec 2027. RED delegated-act cybersecurity rules (in force since Aug 2025) and GPSR (since Dec 2024) have already taught retail compliance teams to demand supplier documents and chase non-EU suppliers, so the workflow and budget owner exist. Retail groups have not yet named a vulnerability-reporting provider, so early mandates set the approved list.
revenue_model: Retailer-paid baseline of EUR 10-25k per range as the first sale. Dashboard licence of EUR 15-40k/yr per retailer. Ten retailers gives roughly EUR 1M+ ARR with sales cost amortised across 60 or more payers per mandate.

Retail supply chains already run on the 'nominated lab' pattern, where the buyer mandates a provider and the supplier pays, and testing spend per product (EN 18031 or similar) dwarfs a EUR 600-1,200 annual desk fee, so suppliers barely resist. The dashboard turns a rare-event insurance product into something a compliance head opens every morning. And retail is the only place where a 24/7 filer has real leverage, because the retailer can delist a supplier that does not respond.

Publish the clause as a free template through retail associations to seed demand. Sign 2 paying baselines by day 30-45. Competitor check: GAP. White space: The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.

- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. title: Vacant-Unit Meter Watchdog and Insurance Vacancy Log
one_liner: Uses utility smart-meter data that owners already have rights to, so PMs can catch squatters, leaks and freeze risk in empty units within hours, without installing any hardware.
customer: Property managers and owners of single-family and 2-to-20-unit portfolios (100 to 2,000 doors). They already pay the utilities on vacant units and carry standard dwelling or small-building policies with a vacancy clause. Buyer is the PM's ops director or the owner. Secondary buyers later are E&S and landlord-program insurers.
problem: When a unit is occupied, the tenant is the sensor and tells you about leaks. When it is vacant you are blind for 20 to 60 days. Water damage, squatters, stolen copper, AC left running and burst pipes all happen in that window. Most property policies restrict vandalism, water damage and theft after roughly 60 days of vacancy, and the claim gets denied or cut exactly when the loss is biggest. Squatter removal is also time-critical: in many states an intruder found on day 2 is a police trespass matter, while the same person on day 30 needs a months-long court eviction. Walk-throughs are weekly at best, and the maintenance tech skips them when busy.
solution: Vacancy Vitals connects to interval electric and water data through owner-authorized utility APIs (Green Button Connect, or aggregators like UtilityAPI). The owner's account is usually the one active during vacancy, so no tenant consent is needed. Rules fire on patterns: continuous 24/7 water flow (leak), electric baseline above the empty-unit norm (someone living there, a crypto miner, a grow), a heating or cooling setpoint far outside range (pipe-freeze or mold risk), and a sudden drop to zero in a unit that should be running HVAC. Alerts go by text to the on-call tech with a one-tap 'send someone' button. The product also generates a time-stamped weekly vacancy-inspection log (data check plus a tech photo check-in) formatted for carriers' vacancy-permit or inspection conditions. That log is what preserves coverage.
why_now: Anti-squatter laws were passed in a wave in 2024 and 2025 (for example Florida and Georgia), which makes early detection more valuable. Smart-meter penetration passed roughly 70% of US electric customers. Insurers have been tightening on water-damage and vacancy exposure for several years. AI-based anomaly detection on interval data is now cheap. (Current state-by-state anti-squatter rules and utility API coverage should be verified before launch.)
revenue_model: $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month on usage, or a flat $1 to $2 per door per month portfolio subscription. Later, insurer-paid or insurer-discounted programs: the carrier pays a fee per monitored door in exchange for lower loss ratios and a vacancy-clause waiver.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest sensor for a vacant house is the meter the utility already installed, and the account is in the owner's name during vacancy. Nobody in proptech treats owner-account utility data as a security and insurance-compliance feed. They sell $60 leak sensors and cameras instead. The other secret is legal timing. The value is not detecting the squatter, it is detecting them in the first 48 hours, when the law treats it as trespass rather than a tenancy.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 to 5 SFR or small-multifamily PMs, offer a free 'backtest', and pull 12 months of interval data for units that were vacant. Show them the incidents the tool would have caught. These are usually a few leaks, a few unauthorized occupants and several HVAC-left-on units, each worth $1,000 to $15,000. Build a UtilityAPI-based prototype with three rules, text alerts and a weekly PDF log. Charge $99 per month per portfolio during the pilot, then convert to per-unit pricing. In parallel, talk to two independent insurance agents who write landlord programs, to learn the exact vacancy-permit language and to get a warm intro for the carrier channel.

competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Arcadia (utility data platform), UtilityAPI, Wint Water Intelligence, SmartRent. White space: I found no product that does what this idea proposes: rules on owner-authorized utility interval data to detect squatters, unauthorized occupancy, leaks and HVAC problems in vacant units, then produce a carrier-formatted vacancy-inspection log with no installed hardware. The alternatives are hardware (Wint, SmartRent, Minut, Flume), utility data plumbing (Arcadia, UtilityAPI), or bill-management tools (Conservice, EnergyCAP). None of their pages pitch vacant-unit security or insurance vacancy compliance. Three things are genuinely unserved: (1) electric-baseline occupancy detection in a vacant unit, which the water-focused players cannot do; (2) an inspection log formatted for carrier vacancy-permit conditions; (3) small portfolios of 100 to 2,000 doors, which Wint and SmartRent do not serve well. I could not find how commonly PMs use utility-supplied continuous-flow leak alerts (water utilities with AMI portals, my background knowledge, unverified). Research limits: the WebSearch budget was used up, so no Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt or forum searches were possible. The verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and background knowledge, and the absence of a direct competitor is not proven. Main risks: (a) UtilityAPI lists $2.40 to $30 per meter per month for scheduled monitoring, so on a $1 to $2 per door or $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month price, data cost could exceed revenue unless you use free Green Button Connect direct integrations or price higher; (b) interval water data through third-party APIs is thin, because most water utilities have no Green Button Connect, and leaks are the biggest loss, so the water rule may only work in a few metros; (c) each owner must authorize each utility account, a real onboarding cost at 100 to 2,000 doors; (d) I found nothing showing carriers accept a monitoring log in place of a vacancy permit or endorsement, so the 'log preserves coverage' claim is unproven; (e) the '48-hour trespass window' insight is unverified. The Florida HB 621 page I fetched confirms sheriff removal and a July 1, 2024 effective date but gives no time threshold, and Wikipedia confirms Alabama's 2024 24-hour removal law, so statute-specific timing needs a lawyer.

title: Refund-Netted Dating: Wholesalers Fund the Float
one_liner: Sell regional wholesalers and buying groups a claim-underwritten '28-day MFP dating' program that defers payment on MFP-drug invoice lines and nets them against the refund, so the pharmacy never borrows and the wholesaler is paid a dilution-risk fee to us.
customer: The independent-pharmacy channel head or CFO at regional full-line wholesalers, independent buying groups and non-wholesaler-owned PSAOs. These are the first wave because they can decide in weeks and cannot out-finance the Big 3 on other terms. The franchise programs of the Big 3 (Good Neighbor Pharmacy, Health Mart, Leader) come second. The pharmacy is the beneficiary, not the payer of record.
problem: The wholesaler owns the weekly auto-debit, the invoice detail and, as a possible third-party support entity, a view into refund flows. It is the cheapest and best-placed capital in the system. But the float squeezes its customers. NCPA-cited behavior includes 70% of pharmacies limiting stock of high-cost drugs and 60% using personal or business savings. That means lost brand volume, rising credit exposure to weakened accounts, and closures (SCPC warns 60% of its members may close). Wholesalers have not extended MFP dating at scale because they see invoices, not claims. They cannot tell which MFP refunds are safe or price the dilution risk of reversals, disputes and 340B rejections. Outside lenders sit behind the wholesaler's debit and cannot fix this.
solution: 'MFP Dating Desk' is software plus a capped dilution guarantee. 1) Connect the wholesaler's invoice and EDI feed with each participating pharmacy's PMS claims export and MTF remittance files, with the pharmacy's consent given inside the wholesaler's normal account flow. 2) Each week, match MFP-drug invoice lines to eligible claims and score dilution risk. 3) The wholesaler moves those lines into a 28-day bucket, or nets them against the refund where it already handles payment routing. 4) We cover dilution losses above the pharmacy's holdback, up to a cap, funded by our reserve and excess capacity from a credit fund or licensed carrier. The guarantee is structured as contractual recourse or through a licensed carrier so it is not unlicensed insurance. 5) The pharmacy sees one dashboard showing what is deferred and when the refund clears. Extended trade terms are commercial credit, not a loan, which avoids most of the lending-license and disclosure work in offspring one.
why_now: In January 2026 the refund lag became a recurring weekly mismatch between 14-day wholesaler terms and a 21-day refund average. On January 1, 2027 semaglutide and 14 other drugs join and the mismatch grows. Independents are choosing wholesalers and buying groups for 2027 terms, so a cash-flow feature is a retention weapon. CMS now expects manufacturers to include cash-flow mitigation in their refund plans, which shows the problem is recognized but unsolved on the distribution side.
revenue_model: The wholesaler pays a platform fee of about $5k a month plus about $10 per active pharmacy, and a risk-and-data fee of about 0.25-0.5% of the deferred refund amount per cycle, calibrated to measured dilution. The wholesaler recovers this through a small service fee. The pharmacy's all-in cost lands near 8-12% annualized, in line with bank A/R lines and well below an MCA. Illustrative: a regional wholesaler with 300 senior-heavy accounts averaging $50k of float has $15M deferred at any time. That is roughly $0.4-0.9M a year of risk fee before losses. Add more wholesalers and buying groups without adding a lending license.
non_obvious_insight: The parent treated the wholesaler as an obstacle. It is actually the best-collateralized lender in the chain, because it holds the debit right, the invoice line item and the relationship. It does not lack capital. It lacks a price for statutory-refund dilution, and that price lives in claim-level data it does not own. Selling underwriting to the party that owns the rails turns a capital-intensive 15-25% lending business into a small fee on a much larger base. It also removes the CAC problem, because the wholesaler's sales reps are the distribution.
first_30_days: List 15 regional wholesalers, buying groups and independent PSAOs and reach the CFO or independent-channel head through association conventions and cold outreach. The pitch is a free 'MFP exposure map' built from their own invoices. Aim for one 60-day shadow pilot with no cash at risk, covering 20-30 senior-heavy accounts. Compare what the deferral would have cost against measured dilution, and use it to set the fee. In parallel, get indicative excess-of-loss terms from one credit fund or specialty carrier and check with counsel whether the guarantee needs a license.
lineage: mutation of I0499 ('Bridge Loans for Medicare Drug-Price Refunds'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: SpendMend (MFP Rebate Reconciliation), Plenful (MFP Intelligence / MFP Command Center), ScriptPro Financial Advantage, Liberty Software (and other PMS vendors, e.g. PioneerRx, PrimeRx, Redsail). White space: Verdict: gap, and a narrow one. In roughly 27 searches across varied terms (MFP refund advance, bridge loan, factoring, fintech, PSAO program, wholesaler program) I found NO product that specifically underwrites and advances against MTF-remitted MFP refunds. Pharmacy lenders sell generic A/R and MCA lines, and the MFP players only sell reconciliation. The unserved space is a claim-level underwriting and servicing capability for refund dilution risk: 340B lesser-of rejections (RARC N907 inappropriate rejections), reversals, Good Faith Inquiry disputes, and authorized-generic refund amounts. It is most valuable for borrowers whose float is large: LTC/senior-care pharmacies, 5-50 store groups, and possibly 340B covered entities in the HRSA rebate pilot, where the float is $8.9M-$208M a year for hospitals (Health Affairs). It also applies to the January 2027 step-up when semaglutide joins.

The wedge is weak in five ways.
1. The 'free missing-refund report' is already crowded: SpendMend, Plenful ($76M raised), ScriptPro, Liberty, and free Beacon MFP dashboards.
2. A typical independent's float is small, about $11k a week or $27k a month per NCPA. At 15-25% APR that is roughly $4-7k a year of gross revenue per pharmacy, before losses and a cost of funds of 8-10%. Customer acquisition through state associations and Facebook groups will be costly relative to that.
3. Wholesalers control the payment path. Cardinal routes MFP refunds through Central Pay and wholesalers auto-debit weekly, so a lender's sweep sits behind the wholesaler in practice. Cardinal customers cannot easily direct refunds to a lender-controlled account.
4. 'Non-recourse' is hard to deliver. Manufacturers can reverse refunds and CMS's own materials describe reversals when claims prove ineligible, so a lender will need pharmacy recourse or holdbacks. That undermines the 'prime paper' insight.
5. Policy is a moving target. CMS made manufacturers include cash-flow mitigation plans in their MFP effectuation plans (accelerated refunds, self-identification). NCPA is still pushing CMS and manufacturers for faster payment, including in Sept 2026 comments on the 2028 guidance.

Adjacent generic lenders can also just add MFP refunds to a borrowing base.

Caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out, so Crunchbase, YC, Product Hunt and open-source sweeps were not fully run. 'No direct competitor found' means not found, not proven absent. | How this version avoids them: Reconciliation vendors (SpendMend, Plenful, ScriptPro, Liberty, Beacon) sell to the pharmacy or health system and end at a report. We sell to the wholesaler and end at a credit decision, so we are not in their category. The Big 3 are listed as adjacent competitors that own the rails. Here they are the eventual channel, not a rival. They can build it but are slow, and the regionals cannot build it at all. No pharmacy borrows, so there is no 15-25% versus 8-12% pricing fight with Live Oak, Corporate Capital Direct, ARF or other lenders, and no borrowing-base conflict with the pharmacy's bank. Wholesaler payment priority is the design, not a risk. The main risk is a Big 3 in-house build. The defenses are speed in the regional segment and a licensable neutral data layer.

title: WhatsApp Voice-Note Superintendent for Spec Builders
one_liner: A bilingual coordinator-plus-AI service that runs daily crew confirmations, headcounts and re-sequencing for a builder's two dozen subs over WhatsApp voice notes, priced per house.
customer: Small private and spec builders (20-300 homes a year) in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, and remodelers who juggle many subs.
problem: A typical home needs about two dozen subs. Foundations sit 30+ days waiting for crews, and one executive described 15-20 houses stuck 6+ weeks. Builders learn a crew is not coming days too late. Project software requires English typing and logins, and workers are wary of anything that looks like tracking. Procore's 20 agents serve larger GCs.
solution: Foremen keep sending Spanish voice notes on WhatsApp. The system transcribes them, extracts headcount, phase status and photos, and updates the schedule. A nearshore bilingual coordinator confirms tomorrow's crews by 5 p.m., calls backup crews when there is a gap, and sends the builder one exception report each morning. Privacy by design: counts and progress only, no IDs or location.
why_now: ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026. Crews can shrink overnight (a Minnesota roofing crew went from 80 to 6). Multilingual speech models and the WhatsApp Business API are mature, and PM incumbents are focused on big GCs.
revenue_model: $300-500 per active house per month, or $3-6K per month per builder. One coordinator handles 25-40 houses, so gross margin is high.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not scheduling math, it is that the people who know whether tomorrow's crew is coming do not use the software. The interface must be the phone and language they already use. The daily headcount is the leading indicator, and knowing a day earlier lets a builder re-sequence trades instead of idling a foundation.
first_30_days: Sign 3 builders with 10-20 active houses each through a home builders association. Hire one bilingual coordinator. Run it manually with WhatsApp and a shared sheet, add speech-to-text in week 2, and document five saved crew-days.

It is unserved partly because it is a labor-arbitrage service business that VC-backed software companies avoid.

title: Scribe-Safe Billing: White-Label Audit for Billing Companies
one_liner: Outsourced billing companies buy a per-provider, coder-signed drift monitor and quarterly attestation letter, then resell it to their small-practice clients as 'scribe-safe billing'.
customer: Mid-size outsourced billing and RCM companies (roughly 40-500 providers under management, spread across 5-50 small groups, for example HBMA members) that bill for practices using a mix of scribes. Later channels: practice-management and EHR marketplaces, and IPAs.
problem: The bulk of scribe adoption in small practices is cheap or low-cost tooling with no compliance officer behind it. The billing company sees every claim across many clients and scribe vendors, is paid a percentage of collections (so scribe uplift raises its own fee), and can be exposed as a party that caused false claims. Its contract says the client owns documentation, but that does not stop a payer or DOJ from asking the biller what it did. Enterprise audit platforms are priced and sold for organizations with in-house compliance staff, so this segment gets nothing. Small groups also lack the resources to appeal payer downcodes.
solution: 'Scribe-Safe' program the biller white-labels. (1) Claims-only monitor across the biller's whole book, with no EHR access: per-provider E/M and modifier drift versus specialty peers, plus the payer downcode rate from 835 remits (CARC 150, 'payer deems the information does not support this level of service') as a leading signal. (2) Quarterly coder-signed review of about 8 encounters per flagged provider, focused on MDM and total-time statements. (3) A signed quarterly attestation letter per practice that the biller can show a client, payer or auditor. (4) A contract addendum plus a refund workflow so findings reach the practice's designated contact and can be acted on within the 60-day overpayment rule, so the biller never sits on an identified problem. (5) Cross-book benchmark by scribe vendor and specialty returned to the biller as a sales asset.
why_now: Small groups adopted low-cost scribes in 2025-26, payers' automated downcoding programs are now hitting the small groups least able to appeal, outsourced billing keeps growing, and billing companies compete on differentiation as AI coding commoditizes their core work. Law-firm commentary warns that 'the AI suggested it' is not a defense. Billing companies now need something independent to point to.
revenue_model: Wholesale $12-20 per provider per month; the biller resells at $25-40 or bundles it for retention. $25 per encounter for extra coder reviews. A 300-provider biller is about $45-70k a year, so 25 billers is roughly $1.1-1.75M ARR. Coder time is about $7 per provider per month at 8 reviews per quarter of about 6 minutes each with an AI pre-read, giving 55-65% gross margin. Land through a 60-day paid pilot at $4-6k per biller.
non_obvious_insight: The payer's own downcode rate is a free, externally labeled audit signal. A jump in CARC 150 adjustments for one provider after go-live means the payer's model has already flagged the notes, before any human looks. The billing company is also the only actor with a cross-client, cross-scribe view, and it buys cover more than detection: an independent signature is the product, which is why more AI coding automation is not a substitute.
first_30_days: Contact HBMA chapter leaders and 40 billing-company owners on LinkedIn. Offer a 60-day paid pilot ($4-6k) that starts with a scan of the biller's aggregated 12-month 837/835 book, structured under the biller's counsel and with the findings routed to practices, not left with the biller. Recruit 2 CPC/CPMA contractors and a healthcare lawyer to draft the addendum and refund workflow. Deliver a provider watchlist and 30 coder-signed reviews to each pilot. Goal: 3 signed pilots and 1 conversion to a per-provider contract.
